table.brief: University rankings: University / Country / Score (Teaching, Research, Citations, Industry) / Overall rank

understanding.purpose: Compare the top seven universities by their overall rank and four component scores, with country providing context.
understanding.reading: Readers identify a university, scan across its row for scores and rank, and compare values down each score column. Longer university names can wrap within their own rows; the two-level header gives the spanning headers room to wrap.
groups: Teaching, Research, Citations and Industry are parallel scores under the shared Score heading and should have comparable widths.
University and Country identify each institution; Overall rank is a separate summary measure.
keep_intact: Individual words in university and country names
may_wrap: Country names at the space between words
Overall rank header between its two words

preferred.name: r2B
preferred.note: Move 11px from Country to University as a smaller adjustment. United Kingdom may wrap, while United States may remain on one line; the extra university space may improve some name breaks without making every country a two-line entry.

acceptable.name: r0A
acceptable.note: Balance room for university names and countries while keeping the four score columns close in width and wrapping the rank header.

acceptable.name: r0B
acceptable.note: Keep country names on one line and give rank more room, accepting additional wrapping in university names.

acceptable.name: r0C
acceptable.note: Favor university names as the main row identifiers, allowing two-word country names and the rank header to wrap.

acceptable.name: r1A
acceptable.note: Refine r0B by moving 13px from Overall rank to University. Keep country names and score headers on one line while giving university names more room; the rank header can still wrap between its two words.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Move 32px from Country to University. This gives long institution names more room and may reduce the Massachusetts entry to two lines, while country names wrap at their word boundary. Preserve the score and rank widths.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Give Country the 132px needed to keep both country names on one line, taking 11px from University. This removes repeated country wrapping while preserving intact score headers and the existing score-column rhythm; check how the narrower university column affects name wrapping.

bad.name: contrast
bad.note: The extra space for university names and rank comes at the expense of the four score columns. Their headers no longer have enough room for intact words, weakening the shared score hierarchy and making comparisons harder to scan.
bad.why: The extra space for university names and rank comes at the expense of the four score columns. Their headers no longer have enough room for intact words, weakening the shared score hierarchy and making comparisons harder to scan.

rationale: r2B keeps every university name to at most two lines while leaving United States on one line; only United Kingdom wraps. The four score headings remain intact and similarly sized, so their values are easy to compare across each row. Its alternating row heights follow the content without the three-line university name seen in r0B and r1A, or the uniformly tall country-driven rows in r0A, r0C and r2A.

general: Give row identifiers enough width to remain recognizable and avoid excessive wrapping.
Columns serving the same comparative role benefit from consistent visual weight and intact headings.
Judge wrapping by its effect on row reading and overall rhythm, rather than minimizing table height alone.
specific: The four score columns need nearly all of their given widths to keep their headings on one line.
A country width near 121px fits United States but wraps United Kingdom; that compromise frees space for the long university names.

tradeoffs: A designer may prefer the regular row heights of r0A, r0C or r2A, or the unwrapped country names in r1A and r3A despite the three-line Massachusetts name. r0B makes the same country tradeoff with less space for university names.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates around r2B, not browser-verified thresholds. They describe individual adjustments with compensating changes elsewhere to keep the total at or below 728px; their maximum values cannot all be used together.

critique.good: The university names remain readable, with the two longest wrapping to two lines. The four score columns form a clear, consistent group, and their headers stay intact.
critique.problems: Every country wraps, making all seven rows tall even when the university name fits on one line. That leaves substantial empty space around the scores.
critique.cause: Country is 105px wide, below the 132px needed for its longest one-line value. University has 210px, while the 72px rank column is already narrow enough to wrap its header.

critique.good: Country names stay on one line, producing compact rows for most institutions. The score headers and values remain intact and easy to compare.
critique.problems: The Massachusetts name takes three lines, and Cambridge also wraps. The resulting mix of row heights makes the university column feel cramped, although the score area remains orderly.
critique.cause: Country receives the 132px needed for one-line values, but University is reduced to 170px. Overall rank has 85px even though its header still wraps.

critique.good: University names have generous space, and the longest names wrap cleanly to two lines. The score columns retain a clear shared rhythm.
critique.problems: Every country wraps, making all rows equally tall and leaving much of the score area empty. The extra university width does not reduce those row heights.
critique.cause: Country is only 82px wide, while University receives 230px. Country therefore determines every row's height.

critique.good: The score columns are closely matched in width, their subheaders stay intact, and the values align clearly for comparison. Country names remain on one line, and the rank column is economical. University names wrap at word boundaries.
critique.problems: The university column feels cramped: Massachusetts occupies three lines, while Cambridge and California occupy two. The resulting uneven row heights interrupt the otherwise compact rhythm, though the rows remain easy to follow.
critique.cause: At 183px, University has 162px for text. Country uses 132px to keep both country names on one line; the score columns and rank are already close to their minimum widths for intact labels.

critique.good: The university column keeps five names on one line, and the four score columns form a clear, compact group. Score headers and values remain intact.
critique.problems: Every country wraps, making every data row two lines tall even when the university name fits on one line. The repeated breaks in United States and United Kingdom make the country column visually busy and spread the scores apart vertically.
critique.cause: At 100px, Country has only 79px of text space, too little for either country name on one line.

critique.good: United States stays on one line, allowing three rows to be shorter. The score columns retain their clear grouping, and all words and score headers stay intact.
critique.problems: United Kingdom still wraps in both of its rows. University of Cambridge also wraps, while the two long institute names occupy two lines; the alternating row heights make the table less regular, though the rows remain easy to follow.
critique.cause: Country has 100px of text space at 121px wide, short of the 111px needed for United Kingdom. Moving 21px from University to Country leaves the 194px university column too narrow for University of Cambridge on one line.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_auto.why: University names and score headers remain intact, and the score columns form a balanced group. Every country wraps, making all rows taller.

contrast.why: The wide university column keeps most names on one line, but all four score headers break inside words, making the comparison labels difficult to scan.

ref_equal.why: The university column is too narrow: Massachusetts breaks inside the word and several names spread over three or four lines, while the score columns have excess space.

r0A.why: The university names wrap naturally, the score headers stay intact, and the score columns are well balanced. Both country names wrap in every row.

r0B.why: Countries and score headers stay on one line, with readable score columns. The narrower university column makes Massachusetts span three lines and Cambridge two.

r2B.why: The widths balance the university names, countries and score headers well. Long university names wrap at word boundaries, most countries fit on one line, and the score columns remain easy to compare.

raw.unsure: The choice between E and F depends partly on whether keeping both country names on one line is more valuable than giving university names more space.

r2B.why: Score headers are intact and evenly spaced, and most countries fit on one line. Three university names wrap, including Cambridge, while United Kingdom wraps.

ref_equal.why: The narrow university column splits Massachusetts within the word and forces several names onto multiple lines, while the score and rank columns have excessive space.

contrast.why: University names have ample room, but all four score headers break inside words and every country wraps, making the score group harder to scan.

r0A.why: The score headers are intact and balanced, and university names wrap at natural word boundaries. Every country occupies two lines.

ref_auto.why: The score columns form a clear, balanced group, and university names wrap cleanly. Countries wrap in every row, adding height throughout.

r0B.why: Countries and score headers stay on one line, giving most rows a compact rhythm. The narrower university column puts Massachusetts on three lines and wraps Cambridge.

raw.unsure: A and F make different reasonable tradeoffs between keeping university names and countries on one line; D and E give the university column more room but wrap every country.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
